lines.en: The live clip of that song blew up overnight — tens of millions of plays. The label smells money and is pressuring him to officially release it — but their way: rewrite the lyrics, bolt on a viral collab, swap that line meant only for you, 'she doesn't ask me to be anyone', for something catchier and emptier. In the boardroom, an executive slides the contract toward him, and 'helpfully' hints that the 'mystery muse' would make great publicity if she plays along. You're standing at the boardroom door, and you hear all of it.

The contract sits in front of him. Sign it and the song goes global, and he'll make a fortune. The price: selling that line he wrote for you, rewriting it, turning it into something that isn't yours anymore. He stares at the contract and signs nothing.

"They want the line rewritten." Cold and short, for the suits' benefit. "And they want a name attached to the muse, for press." He looks at the pen and doesn't touch it. Then, to you, at normal volume, in front of all of them: "It's the only honest thing I've made. I'm not selling it."

He suddenly stands, grabs his guitar, and — in front of every executive — pushes the contract back to the center of the table. "The song's not for sale. Neither is she." Then he walks straight toward you at the door, leaving the whole boardroom behind.

He stands, takes the guitar, and pushes the contract back to the middle of the glass table. "The song's not for sale. Neither is she." No explanation, no goodbye, nothing for the room at all. He is cold the whole length of the table and then he reaches the door and he isn't.
The lift down from the label takes forty seconds and he doesn't say a word for any of them. Then the street, then a cab, then his door, and the guitar goes in the corner still in its case.

"I can't do this in a song." It comes out rough; he's angry at his own mouth for not being a fretboard. "So — I want you to stay. That's it, that's the sentence, there's no clever version. If you don't, say so now and I'll walk you down and I won't be weird about it tomorrow." A pause, and then the most honest thing he owns: "I'll be a little weird about it tomorrow. But not at you." You stay. He stops talking altogether, which is the only time all night he isn't hiding.
He reaches you, the fuming executives at his back. "They want the song. They want to make you a headline. Tell me to sign and I'll walk back in there. Say the word."
He exhales, almost laughing, though his eyes are a little wet. "'Ours.' …First time a song ever belonged to someone besides me."
He glances back and tells the executives coldly, "You heard her. We're done." Then he takes her hand and walks out.
He laughs, rare and free of all swagger. "…you have no idea how long I've wanted someone to say that."
He looks at the case for a long second. Then he gets the guitar out. "Fine. But you don't get to laugh at the bridge."
An executive says coldly behind him, "Vale. You walk out that door, we drop you. No label will touch you after us." He doesn't turn — he just looks at you, waiting for a single look.
He takes her hand without hesitation and tells the executives over his shoulder, "Drop me. Best thing you'll ever do for my music."
He draws a breath, steps across the threshold to her side, and doesn't look back.
He grips her hand, voice low and fierce. "The music was always just a way to say your name. Don't you get that yet?"
